subject: Request Guidance--Diagnosing R Crash from cfa()

messages.author: 57e91be86af77659
messages.subject: Request Guidance--Diagnosing R Crash from cfa()
parts:
I have a study in which I am calling cfa() many, many times--1200 times in one program, 3600 times in another program.  During the course of running the program, R crashes with regularity with the error "R for Windows GUI front-end has stopped working."  Once I acknowledge that error, the R session closes.  So I am not able to run any sort of trace-back.  I have been trying for about a week to isolate a case that repeats the problem to no avail.   I am hoping you can provide some suggestions as to how I can identify a test case that I can make available to you.
 
I have commented out the call to cfa() (and all the commands that come after it that use the results) and find that my program runs without problem.  When I un-comment the call to cfa() (without un-commenting anything else), it crashes again.  If I re-run the program, it may crash again, but never on the same data set.  I have tried running a single data set 10000 times.  It runs without problem.  I have found that the object returned by cfa() can be quite large--up to 169 Mb.  I have tried deleting the object as soon as I have extracted the needed information.  I have monitored the memory occupied by the R session, and it does not come close to the amount that memory.size() says is available. 
 
I am at a loss as to what else to check.
 
I am running lavaan 0.5-16 under R 3.0.2 64-bit on a Windows machine running Windows 7.
 
I hope you can help me narrow down this problem.  Thank you for your consideration.
 
Sincerely.
Lisa Henn

Hello Lisa!

I am glad you bring this up. I, too, had the exact same error while running simulations in lavaan a while back. Here's the link:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/8ncLFuKYzuE

What I learned from the error is that, unfortunately, it does not appear unless one calls lavaan several hundred times (in my case the problem was with the simulateData() function.

I tried everything  and by that I mean EVERYTHING to make it go away: upgrading lavaan, downgrading lavaan, upgrading R, downgrading R, running R with no packages but lavaan, running it in several computers to no avail. Once the error showed up it would never go away. I learned that if you do your analyses in RStudio you can "buy yourself some time" (i.e. you can run a few thousand runs before RStudio crashes as well). What I've found is that it's difficult for others to reproduce this error because you need to be running lavaan (on a Windows machine) several thousand times for a while before it appears. But once it appears it doesn't seem to go away (which makes running simulations in lavaan a real pain). 

Eventually I gave up and ran my simulations in a MAC computer, since this seems to be a Windows-only issue.

parts: I have tried running a single data set 10000 times.  It runs without problem.

You can fit a model to the same data.frame 10,000 times, but you can't fit that model to 10,000 different data.frames without R crashing?  I find that very curious.  Would you be able to post your program so someone could try to replicate your (I assume) simulation?  Or at least a simplified version of it?  Also, it might be helpful to post the output from sessionInfo() in case it is a software/version issue.  And in case it is a memory/hardware issue, info about your RAM and processor might be helpful.

Terry

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Request Guidance--Diagnosing R Crash from cfa()
parts:
Lisa,

Would you be willing to send me your full R script? (One that causes R
to crash). That would allow me to investigate the matter.

I run a lot of simulation studies myself. Sometimes, lavaan() is called
>1million times in a single job. Sometimes, the data.frames are >2GB in
size. My major concern until now was that lavaan was sometimes very slow
(not being a compiled package). But it never crashed.

BUT, this is all under linux. Or on a high performance cluster, and all
nodes run linux again. It would seem this is a windows only issue, but
even if it is, we still need to resolve it, or at least try to
understand why it happens.

Are you using the predict() function? Do you have categorical data? This
would explain the call to lav_predict_fy_eta.i, which --at the moment
(0.5-16)-- is perhaps one of the least-optimized functions in lavaan: it
is called multiple times (trying to find good values for the latent
variables) for each row in a data.frame. What happens if you do not call
predict()? Do you need those predictions for all cases?

Some things you may try (although I have no reason to believe they may
have an effect in your setting):

- when using rm(), always call the garbage collector, gc()
- if you generate datasets, delete them when they are not needed anymore
- avoid attaching other packages (like mirt, which also loads parts of
Rcpp via the namespace)


About the size of a fitted lavaan object: it stores an internal copy of
the data. But if you get an object that is 162Mb, and you delete it, and
the workspace is only 0.4Mb, what happened to the original data? Is it
still in the workspace? That would another thing that interests me:
could you send me a script that produces this object of size 162Mb
(without having anything else in the workspace, except the data and the
model)?

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Request Guidance--Diagnosing R Crash from cfa()
parts:
On 06/16/2014 03:57 AM, Lisa Henn wrote:
> as a script that produces the 169 Meg object returned from cfa()

I had a look at the object size (169Mb). Most of this is due to a slot
(called `CAT', part of object@SampleStats) where I store a lot of
intermediate results that are used to compute the weight (WLS.V) matrix.
Strictly speaking, this object is completely redundant. I will remove it
in a next update. This will reduce the size to about 52.7Mb. Still a
large object. It contains to large matrices: the 'WLS.V' matrix (good
for 25.6Mb), and the 'NACOV' matrix (also 25.6Mb).

But we should realize that the weight matrix, with 60 items, has a
dimension: 1830 x 1830. That is a big matrix. The same for NACOV:
another matrix of 1830 x 1830.

This explains the large object size. But not the crash.

Yves.

messages.author: 326bbae8902de59c
messages.subject: Re: Request Guidance--Diagnosing R Crash from cfa()
parts:
It's good news that the object returned by cfa() can be made smaller.  That surely will be an improvement.
 
As I promised, I ran the program that has the call to Rprofmem() in it.  I commented out the command to load the mirt library and the loop that handles the all the mirt work.  I also commented out the call to predict() and everything downstream of it that is affected by that call.  I also added a call to gc() immediately after I remove the object returned from cfa().
 
This version of the program crashed on the 1135th call to cfa().  (It almost made it to the end.)  I have extracted the last 200 lines of the Rprofmem.out file.  Please find it attached. 
 
The script that I had sent that produces the 169 Mb object returned from cfa() is the script I had written to call cfa() 10,000 times.  When I had run it before, I had used a different data set than the one that produces the 169 Mb returned object.  The data set I originally chose was from a simulation condition that produced crashes in the main simulation, but for which the call to cfa() was relatively quick.  In these past few days, I re-ran the script with this other data set, the one that produces the 169 Mb object.  Now the script crashes.
 
I edited the script to remove the object returned from cfa() as well as add the garbage collector gc().  I also added the command to load the mirt library.  So far, the script has successfully called cfa() over 600 times.  I will let it continue to run, as it is not harming anything.  I expect it to crash, though, probably in the range of 800 - 1200 calls to cfa().
 
It would seem that adding the garbage collector helps.  Not calling predict() probably also helps.  It seems that loading the mirt library has no discernible effect.  It remains to be seen whether calls to any functions from the mirt library has an adverse effect.
 
I do not have sufficient familiarity with the details of the lavaan functions to intuit what to try next based on the attached output.  I hope this output either illuminates the source of the trouble or suggests other things to try.
 
Thank you again for your assistance.  You have been helpful and responsive on all the issues I have encountered.  The project leader asked me to convey her appreciation as well.    
 
Regards,
Lisa
